title: Breaking and Entering: Now or Never with Elise Peyronnet
transcript:
Elise Peyronnet, Artistic Director of Now or Never, joined Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studio to discuss the festival's 2026 program. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 2 July 2026.

Lauren: The Artistic Director of the festival, Elise Peyronnet, is with me in the studio. Hey, Elise.

Elise: Hi, Lauren.

Lauren: Lovely to catch up with you again. You and I go way back to your Melbourne Music Week days, many, many moons ago.

Elise: That's true, actually. We've known each other for a little while. But thank you so much for having me today.

Lauren: Thank you for joining me. An incredible line-up that you've put together for what is now the fourth year of the festival, which was originally born as a combination of Melbourne Music Week and Melbourne Knowledge Week, combining forces, and now is City of Melbourne's annual festival spanning art, ideas, sound and technology. We'll get into some of the specifics of some of the events in a moment. But to start, this year's curatorial theme for Now or Never is A Whole New World. Can you tell me about your vision as the Artistic Director, and how that theme shapes this year's program?

Elise: Well, the theme was chosen many, many months ago. And I guess, as the world unfolded, and just looking at everything that's happening geopolitically, we are absolutely in a whole new world. But initially, the theme was really talking to, I guess, the technological shifts that we are seeing in our everyday life. Of course, we talk a lot about AI, and we are only just starting to see the impact of it. So I think we wanted to have a theme that was broad enough to really discuss that fact, and maybe not necessarily fearing it, but just mentioning that we are indeed in a whole new world.

And I think for a curatorial theme, in terms of talks, it's interesting to cover that. But also in terms of even creating events, there are a lot of the events around the city where we are going to take over buildings, and change maybe the experience that people will have from the different areas in the city. And that is also inviting the audience to step into a whole new world.

Lauren: You mentioned AI, being a festival that covers technology as one of its core pillars. So I imagine your curatorial team and programming team are having some big conversations around that as well, with the ways in which we understand knowledge feeling like they're being reshaped at the moment. How have you been navigating that current shift, and the ways that it's reflected within the program?

Elise: I mean, yes, it's a current theme, and one that we're, I think, still grappling with. It's a really hot topic for artists as well. I know that we have also discussed this topic since the beginning of Now or Never. In fact, Now or Never was created in 2023, so already in 2022 it was really the beginning also of AI in everyday life. So it's always been a core topic, but I think we question it, but it is here. Probably all of us use it every day, in everyday life. But it is indeed scary when it's brought to the light of, in an artistic sense, does it replace really the human agency and the artistic expression or not? And it's just a tool that can enhance. We're still at the beginning of that conversation.

Lauren: Totally. And there's a few events happening as part of the program that do reflect on that, for sure. The festival itself runs across 12 days. Now or Never is a huge program: more than 250 local and international artists and creatives. You've got over 150 events. Where do you start putting a program like this together? Was there a particular moment for you that locked in first with the program?

Elise: It always comes from the venues, the locations. And we have now worked, since the beginning, with creating really unique experiences at the Royal Exhibition Building. So I think that's one of the concepts that we started to work on, but that took a really long time to come to fruition. So again, spaces, and looking at the city and where we want to place things: I think it always, for me, starts there.

Lauren: The City of Melbourne, the Now or Never festival, has a reputation for commissioning this really unique site-specific work. I imagine there's some creative challenges, maybe, with programming these cutting-edge technology events inside these buildings that are centuries old, like the Royal Exhibition Building and Melbourne Town Hall. What sort of creative challenges have you faced?

Elise: In fact, every year is a different one, but again, this year it's a completely different take on the Royal Exhibition Building. And we are bringing back a series of music, and a series of really slow-paced, meditative shows that are really kind of taking the counterpart of technology, in a way. If anything, it is about slowing down and being in the moment. And I think that was an interesting balance to have in the program as well. So if anything, in a way, we are going without technology — or it's not without technology, but really thinking about being in the present, and really experiencing music in a different way.

Lauren: Speaking of slowing down, there's an event that's slowing down so much, it's a mass sleepover slumber party, where you have the opportunity to sleep over at the Royal Exhibition Building, with an event called Somnia, which sounds pretty incredible. Can you talk us through that particular event?

Elise: Yes, so this is indeed quite a unique experience, where we invite the audience to come and take a bed. At the Royal Exhibition Building, we will have a durational concert show with multiple artists. We have first Bendik Giske, who is an amazing saxophonist, but experimental artist, who has worked with Caterina Barbieri, has really reinvented saxophone as an instrument. And it's quite a physical experience. You can hear him breathe through the instrument. This is the first part of the night.

And after that, we have invited William Basinski, amazing American experimental composer, to come and perform continuously the series of four albums that he created, The Disintegration Loops, that are really a landmark ambient work for a lot of music lovers. So we were really looking for a piece of music that could have that pace, where we are inviting reflection and meditation. The music is quite melancholic. It's actually about disappearing. It's about digitising the tapes, actually, the music that he had created. And as he's playing them, the loops are disappearing, and the music is disappearing. So it's a very profound piece of music as well. So it will go for six hours. You can decide to stay up, move around the venue, or take the bed and just stay there.

Lauren: And when you say take the bed, people don't have to bring their own bed.

Elise: Sorry. Take the bed that you would have been assigned to. And then we'll have a wake-up moment, and a little breakfast final moment before people exit the venue.

Lauren: That sounds incredible. I actually listened to the whole of — or one of the tracks of William Basinski's The Disintegration Loops last night, in preparation for this interview. And it's believed to have influenced many artists, including Burial, as an example, as well. What sort of things are you needing to consider to support the audience through such an intense sonic experience over those 10 hours?

Elise: I think we just want to give some comfort for the audience. I think it's important. I think you experience music in a completely different way when you are lying down. I think it's also linking maybe to the deep listening experiences that are really blossoming everywhere. There's a lot more at the moment, because maybe people are looking for a different way of taking in the music. And I think that's what we are trying to emulate. We're trying to really create an environment that will be conducive to this.

Lauren: Is this a work that you've experienced yourself before bringing this to Melbourne, or…?

Elise: No, no. I've always wanted to do a sleep event. Of course, we looked at Max Richter, who performed before in Australia. But this was curated especially for Melbourne, with Melbourne in mind. And yes, the first of maybe many. We'll see how we go this year.

Lauren: I'm sure you'd be advising people coming along to rug up as well, given it's the middle of winter in Melbourne, in the Royal Exhibition Building.

Elise: Yes, yes, it's BYO for the bedding.

Lauren: And for fans of Philip Glass, there's a homage to the world-renowned American composer as well, as part of the festival. Can you tell us about that event?

Elise: Yeah, again, this has been curated as part of a full series around that meditative state. And I mean, Philip Glass's music is that beautiful, repetitive, minimalist music. He has influenced so many different composers in so many different genres. And I think when we program music, we're always looking for bringing some diversity as well, and not just having electronic-based music. We're an art and technology festival, but we're also looking at innovation and experimentation as being really the key driving factors for us programming some of those acts.

And Philip Glass, very amazing, amazing composer, as I was saying. I really wanted to bring that music that is usually presented in concert halls into a different environment, being the Royal Exhibition Building. We have the stage in the centre, under the dome, with the audience around it, seated. And I wanted it to be accessible to as many people as possible who may want to discover that music. We have first Orchestra Victoria. We have close to 30 musicians on stage, performing a unique piece of Philip Glass that is rarely performed alone. It's a ballet piece initially. And then we have Maki Namekawa, who is this fantastic pianist, soloist, who has worked with Philip Glass, collaborated with him. And she's going to perform the piano etudes one to 10, which are really, really, again, landmark piano works. But piano, again, is very accessible. And it's going to be a really beautiful night.

Lauren: Gorgeous. And Elise, there's also a headline late-night music program at Melbourne Town Hall that features a whole bunch of artists across three nights, both local and international. Can you take us through some of the things happening at Melbourne Town Hall?

Elise: Yes. So Town Hall is going to be transformed for the full duration of the festival, going to take different shapes. We have Robin Fox first, who has a new commission piece, a new piece, who's going to take over the main hall. It's an installation, lots of lasers. It's all around the room. That is during the week, free for the public to come. We have invited [name uncertain] to also present a new work, a new dance work, inside Town Hall as well. So that's to start the festival.

And then as we move into the second weekend, we change over the venue again into more of a music venue. So we have three nights, where two of them we've invited local promoters. We really wanted to, maybe in the spirit of Melbourne Music Week and how we have worked in the past with lots of our amazing independent promoters that we have here in Melbourne. And we've invited Chuleo Club, which are amazing, promoting Latinx, Latin club, underground music, and have been doing that for many years, mainly at Miscellania in Melbourne. But we really wanted to profile them and work with them. They've curated an amazing line-up. We have [name uncertain: Aisha], we have Dinamarca, some artists that have actually never played here in Melbourne before. So very excited about that. And Zalina, who is the head honcho, I guess, of Chuleo Club, will be also performing.

And on the Saturday we have Octave One, amazingly legendary Detroit producers, that are playing live. It's a really great live show, very big and fun to watch. And in fact, the entire night is mainly built around artists playing with hardware equipment. So we have Sleep D as well, and Hybrid Man, who is going to come and perform on that night, and Jeanette as well. And then to close on the Sunday, we are bringing back My Disco, who I think have not been performing for many years. So it's kind of their return with us. We're very excited about having them back.

Lauren: What did you say to My Disco to get them to reform for you?

Elise: I think it was just apparently the right time. I think they were ready. They wanted to. It didn't really take that much, I don't know…

Lauren: Convincing.

Elise: Convincing, maybe. And maybe what helped as well was that we knew that we had Robin Fox closing as well. And they're close in their relationships and artistic endeavours. So I think maybe that's what I would say: that it's Robin who influenced their decision.

Lauren: And there's also Derrick Gee's Radio Hour, who's been a guest on this program before. His show is all about deep listening, which Melbourne Recital Centre is really going to be the perfect venue for, that experience in that acoustically treated room. Can you tell us about the concept for that show and what audiences can expect?

Elise: Yes, I agree that the venue is going to lend itself really well too. It's really intimate. It's like an old-school, in a way, radio show. I mean, Derrick Gee, for those who don't know him, is an internet personality. He has interviewed amazing artists, international big names, smaller names, but he's just really good at being able to explain music to anyone, really. He really embodies what a music critic could be, but in a really conversational way. So he has put together his night. He's inviting Julia Jacklin, who's going to be coming, chatting with him, performing, playing some tracks, and Michael Kucyk, who is the boss of Efficient Space. Amazing line-up, label as well. So a really great night of chats in a living room environment.

Lauren: Very cool. And I should say, as a bit of a disclaimer, through my work at the Wheeler Centre as a programmer, I have been involved in some of the talks, putting the talks program together with your team at Now or Never as well. But there was one I wanted to particularly mention that might be of some interest to RRR listeners, as it features a line-up of speakers that are very near and dear to many RRR listeners. Including Sosefina Fuamoli, Sarah Smith as well, Al Newstead, who's written a book recently as part of the 33⅓ series on Tame Impala's Currents, and hosted by a good friend of this show, Simon Winkler, who of course was the co-host of Breaking and Entering for 18 years. They're coming together for what should be a really fascinating conversation on music criticism that's happening at the Wheeler Centre too. So much to discover as part of Now or Never as well. Of course, there's some incredible large-scale light installations happening along the Birrarung/Yarra River as well. Is there anything else in particular you'd like to draw our attention to as part of the program, some of your favourite others?

Elise: I think there are different layers, different ways of interacting, I hope, with Now or Never. We have a really large program of free, amazing installations all around the city. You mentioned Southbank, and we have some projections onto Hamer Hall. We have an amazing artist, Aka Chang from Taiwan, who's coming for the first time, presenting also a laser installation on the river, reflecting onto the river. We have Emily Parsons-Lord, who is an amazing artist based in Melbourne as well, who's going to make the Evan Walker Bridge disappear in mist. So there will be lots of really large-scale installations all around there. And then if you start from Melbourne Town Hall with Robin Fox, you'll be able to have a full experience of the city being all lit up, and really seeing amazing artists brought, I think, on a bigger scale. And some really great local talent as well.

Lauren: Incredible. Well, congratulations, Elise, on another amazing program this year. Now or Never takes over the city from August 19 to 30. Our guest has been the artistic director, Elise Peyronnet from Now or Never. Thanks so much, Elise.

Elise: Thank you, Lauren.
